title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space
formal:
Does there exist one computable compiler \(\mathcal C\) that maps every deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) to a reversible multitape machine \(R=\mathcal C(M)\) with the following simultaneous guarantees? For every \(M\), there are a constant \(c_M\ge1\) and an integer \(d_M\ge1\) such that, on every input \(x\) on which \(M\) halts, \(R\) halts with exactly the output pair \((x,M(x))\), clears its auxiliary tapes, and satisfies
\[S_R(x)\le c_M S_M(x),\qquad T_R(x)\le c_M T_M(x)^{d_M}.\]
On every input on which \(M\) does not halt, \(R\) must also fail to halt. The same \(R\) must meet both bounds on every halting input. This is the previously selected polynomial-time, linear-space version of the source's broader simulation tradeoff question.
definitions:
Each machine has a finite transition table, finitely many states, a finite tape alphabet containing 0, 1, a blank and delimiters, and a fixed finite number of two-way tapes with one head per tape. A transition reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes are indexed by integers, and all heads initially sit at a designated origin. The machine description lists these finite objects explicitly in a fixed effectively decodable binary syntax. Alphabet size, tape count and states may depend on the fixed machine but not on its input. There are no oracle, advice, random or external-storage tapes.

Initially the binary input \(x\), with fixed delimiters, occupies consecutive cells of one tape; all other cells are blank. A halting run has a finite designated binary output \(M(x)\), with delimiters on an output tape. A transition is a partial deterministic function on full configurations; a configuration with no next transition is terminal. The full configuration includes the state, every tape's contents and every head position. A simulator must implement the stated terminal-output convention on its intended input runs.

A machine is reversible if its partial one-step map is injective on its entire configuration space: whenever transitions from configurations \(u\) and \(v\) produce the same configuration, \(u=v\). Thus no step may merge two different predecessor configurations. This property concerns the finite machine's full transition semantics, not just the particular run from a blank workspace. Halting states have no outgoing step; injectivity does not require every configuration to have a predecessor. Reversibility is logical reversibility of a classical machine, not a physical energy model or a quantum operation.

For a halting run, \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct tape cells initially occupied or visited during the entire run, summed over all tapes, with a minimum of 1. A cell still counts if it is later erased. Input, output, delimiter, history and work cells all count. Let
\[T_M(x)=\max\{1,|x|,\text{number of transitions before halting}\}.\]
Define \(S_R,T_R\) in exactly the same way. This is a per-input resource comparison, not a comparison of unrelated worst-case inputs of a given length. Finite control is part of the fixed machine description, while every tape cell used at run time is included. No additional initially full catalytic tape is supplied for free.

At termination, the simulator has two designated output tracks or tapes containing the original \(x\) and \(M(x)\), with the fixed delimiters, and all auxiliary tape contents are blank. Retaining \(x\) is essential: different inputs can yield the same \(M(x)\), but a reversible computation cannot merge their histories into an identical final configuration. The output pair is required exactly; leaving a computation-history string as garbage is not accepted. The simulator need only preserve the partial function in this input-preserving sense, rather than reproduce each intermediate configuration of \(M\).

The compiler is a single total deterministic computable function on valid machine descriptions; its compilation time is unrestricted. It outputs a finite reversible machine description, with no dependence on the later input \(x\). Neither the compiler nor the simulator is given the eventual halting time or space use as an extra input. The constants \(c_M,d_M\) may depend on \(M\), but are fixed before quantifying over all \(x\). No halting-time or resource bound is required on divergent runs beyond preservation of nontermination. A simulator chosen separately for every individual input would not satisfy the compiler requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this compiler. A positive answer must establish total computability of compilation, reversibility of every output machine on its full configuration space, preservation of the partial function and nontermination behavior, clean input-preserving output, and the two simultaneous per-input resource bounds. A negative answer must prove that no compiler can satisfy these requirements for all machines and inputs; failure of one known construction does not suffice. Separate simulators achieving the time and space bounds independently do not settle the conjunction. A lower bound only for reversible pebble games, an oracle-relative simulation model or circuits does not refute unrestricted reversible multitape simulation. The resource requirements are exact asymptotic claims, without additive numerical tolerance.
why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: An irreversible computation may overwrite information that is no longer needed. A reversible machine must retain enough information elsewhere to make each transition invertible on its image. The question asks whether doing so can always preserve the original storage scale while incurring only polynomial time overhead.

Input preservation and clearing auxiliary tapes specify what counts as a completed simulation. They prevent two easy ambiguities: erasing distinct inputs that have the same answer, and treating a large retained execution history as an acceptable final result.

Bennett’s simulations establish polynomial-time reversible computation with space \(O(S\log(T+2))\), among other tradeoffs. The logarithmic multiplier is not bounded by one machine-dependent constant as the input grows, so this bound does not establish the card’s \(O(S)\) requirement.

Lange, McKenzie and Tapp show that deterministic space can be preserved by reversible computation. The general construction can take exponential time, so space preservation alone does not imply the required polynomial overhead in the original running time.

Buhrman, Tromp and Vitányi give intermediate time-space tradeoffs and discuss how to remove an advance bound on the simulated running time. Their result bridges the classical extremes but does not give the required simultaneous polynomial-time and constant-factor-space guarantee for every machine.

Reversible pebble games model a particular style of simulation, with memory snapshots represented by pebbles. A lower bound for that model need not apply to all reversible machines. The space-preserving theorem itself demonstrated that general simulation can escape restrictions of that particular model.

The 2026 catalytic-computation paper studies an additional tape initialized with arbitrary contents that must be restored. Its reversible-space lemma has no general polynomial-time-overhead guarantee. Both its separate catalytic resource and the missing time bound matter: it is related progress, not a solution to the total-storage target here.

Logical reversibility is relevant to the information erased during computation, but this card does not set an energy bound for hardware. Its mathematical success criterion is entirely the classical compiler, correctness, time and space statement.

progress.text: Bennett establishes input-preserving reversible simulations with polynomial time and an additional logarithmic space factor, among other tradeoffs.
Lange–McKenzie–Tapp preserve deterministic space under reversibility without a simultaneous general polynomial-time guarantee.
Theorem 1 gives a time-space tradeoff between classical extremes; §5.3 handles initially unknown computation time.
The survey retains simultaneous efficient time and space simulation as a main open problem.
The catalytic-computation paper’s appendix uses reversible space simulation in a distinct storage model, without the simultaneous time guarantee requested here.

sentences: The question asks whether every deterministic computation can be compiled into a reversible one with polynomial time overhead and only a constant-factor space increase.
The simulator preserves the input and exact output, clears auxiliary storage and retains nontermination on divergent inputs.
Time and space are compared on the same input, and input, output and history storage all count.
Known general simulations attain the two desired efficiencies separately or with a tradeoff, while catalytic-space results use a different resource model.
A complete answer must prove or refute one computable compiler meeting all of these guarantees simultaneously.
